extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and researchers studying mathematical logic and computability (incompleteness, provability)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository treatment of Gödel incompleteness, representability of computable relations, derivability predicates (Prf/Prov), Rosser's trick, Löb's theorem, and the undefinability of truth for theories extending Q/PA. Focus is on precise definitions, lemmas, and proof sketches used to establish undecidability and incompleteness results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory is consistent if it does not prove both α and ¬α for any formula α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inconsistent theory is trivial (every sentence is provable). Consistency is a minimal requirement used throughout: many results assume consistency or use inconsistency to derive contradictions in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: ω-consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∃x α(x) is any sentence and T derives ¬α(0), ¬α(1), ¬α(2), . . . then T does not prove ∃x α(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every ω-consistent theory is consistent (contrapositive: an ω-inconsistent theory may still be consistent). Gödel's original incompleteness used ω-consistency to show T neither proves nor refutes the Gödel sentence; Rosser later relaxed this to simple consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatizable theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory T is said to be axiomatizable if it has a computable set of axioms A (i.e., T = {α : A ⊢ α}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any theory with a finite set of axioms is axiomatizable. If A is computable, then T is computably enumerable (Lemma 184A): one can search for derivations from A to decide membership in T in a c.e. way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computably enumerable (c.e.) theory
rubrics_metrics.description: If T is axiomatizable (has a computable set of axioms A), then T is computably enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: to determine if α ∈ T, search for a derivation of α from A. Put differently, α ∈ T iff there exists a finite list of axioms β1,...,βk in A and a derivation of (β1 ∧ · · · ∧ βk) → α, a property that is c.e.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory is complete if for every sentence α, either α or ¬α is provable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete + axiomatizable implies decidable (Lemma 185A): simultaneously search for a proof of α and a proof of ¬α; one will be found and consistency ensures you can answer. This ties completeness to decidability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidable theory (undecidability results)
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory T is decidable if the set of sentences provable in T is a decidable set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key results: any consistent theory extending Q is not decidable (Theorem 183B for consistent, 182B for ω-consistent), and any theory consistent with Q is undecidable (Theorem 188A). Corollaries: true arithmetic, first-order logic in many languages, and any consistent extension of ZFC are undecidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of computable functions/relations in Q
rubrics_metrics.description: If T includes Q, then T (and Q) represents the computable functions and relations (T represents Kleene's T relation and Prf relation, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This representability is used to internalize computability notions (e.g., PrfT(x,y), δdiag representing diagonalization). Representability allows moving from meta-mathematical statements about computations to formal sentences in the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: No universal computable relation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no binary computable relation R(x,y) such that whenever S(y) is a unary computable relation there is k with S(y) equivalent to R(k,y) for all y (Lemma 183A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses diagonalization: take S(y) = ¬R(y,y) to obtain contradiction. This lemma underlies nonexistence-of-universal-enumerators arguments used in undecidability proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prf and Prov predicates (representability of proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prf_T(x,y) holds iff x is the Gödel number of a derivation of the wff with Gödel number y in T; Prf_T is decidable/representable in Q and T. Define Prov_T(y) as ∃x Prf_T(x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representability of Prf_T and Prov_T in the theory is central to constructing self-referential sentences (Gödel sentences) and formalizing statements like 'y is provable in T.' The theory must be strong enough to reason about proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-point lemma (diagonalization / self-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let T be any theory extending Q, and let β(x) be any wff with only the variable x free. Then there is a sentence α such that T ⊢ α ↔ β(⌜α⌝).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses a representable diagonalization function δdiag. The lemma provides a general method to produce sentences that assert properties about their own Gödel numbers; used to build Gödel and Rosser sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gödel sentence and its unprovability
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists χ_T such that Q (and hence T) derives χ_T ↔ ¬Prov_T(⌜χ_T⌝). If T is a consistent, axiomatizable theory extending Q, then T ⊬ χ_T (Lemma 192A). If T is ω-consistent and axiomatizable, then T ⊬ ¬χ_T as well (Lemma 192C), so T is incomplete (Theorem 192D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: χ_T says 'χ_T is not derivable in T.' The unprovability (and, with ω-consistency, unrefutability) yields incompleteness. Rosser's trick later replaces ω-consistency by simple consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rosser provability and Rosser's theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Ref_T(x,y) for refutations and let RProv_T(y) be ∃x (Prf_T(x,y) ∧ ∀z (z < x → ¬Ref_T(z,y))). By the fixed-point lemma there is ρ_T with Q ⊢ ρ_T ↔ ¬RProv_T(⌜ρ_T⌝). For any consistent, axiomatizable theory T extending Q, T is not complete (Theorem 193A): T neither proves ρ_T nor ¬ρ_T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RProv_T(y) encodes 'there is a proof of y and no shorter refutation of y.' Rosser's construction avoids the need for ω-consistency; it shows simple consistency suffices for incompleteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computable inseparability of Q and ¯Q
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ¯Q = {α : Q ⊢ ¬α}. Q and ¯Q are computably inseparable: there is no computable C with Q ⊆ C and ¯Q ⊆ C (Lemma 187A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof builds a universal computable relation from such a separator, yielding a contradiction. This shows an intrinsic algorithmic indistinguishability between provable and refutable sentences in Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theories consistent with Q are undecidable
rubrics_metrics.description: If T is any theory in the language of arithmetic that is consistent with Q (i.e., T ∪ Q is consistent), then T is undecidable (Theorem 188A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses finite conjunction φ of Q's axioms and defines C = {α : T ⊢ φ → α} to separate Q and ¯Q if T were decidable; contradiction. Consequence: first-order logic for arithmetic language and many foundational theories (e.g., ZFC) are undecidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretability of Q in a theory implies undecidability
rubrics_metrics.description: If a theory T can interpret the language of arithmetic so that T is consistent with the interpretation of Q (or proves the interpretation of Q's axioms), then T is undecidable; no consistent extension of such T is decidable (Theorem 189A and Corollaries 189B–D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: ZFC interprets arithmetic, so there is no decidable extension of ZFC and no complete, consistent, computably axiomatizable extension of ZFC. Also yields undecidability criteria for languages with certain symbol types (e.g., binary relation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivability conditions (P1–P3) for Prov predicate
rubrics_metrics.description: For a suitable Prov_T(y) in a sufficiently strong theory (e.g., PA) the following hold: P1. If PA ⊢ α, then PA ⊢ Prov_PA(⌜α⌝). P2. PA ⊢ Prov_PA(⌜α → β⌝) → (Prov_PA(⌜α⌝) → Prov_PA(⌜β⌝)). P3. PA ⊢ Prov_PA(⌜α⌝) → Prov_PA(⌜Prov_PA(⌜α⌝)⌝).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions formalize basic properties of provability (closure under derivation, modus ponens, and provability of provability) and are required for the second incompleteness theorem and Löb's theorem. P4 (if PA ⊢ Prov(⌜α⌝) then PA ⊢ α) may hold for some representations but is not needed here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency statement Con_T
rubrics_metrics.description: Con_T is formalized as ¬Prov_T(⌜0 = 1⌝) (e.g., Con_PA = ¬Prov_PA(⌜0 = 1⌝)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second Incompleteness Theorem (Theorem 196A/196B): If T is a consistent theory extending Q and Prov_T satisfies P1–P3, then T does not derive Con_T. Intuition: a sufficiently strong, consistent theory cannot prove its own consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Löb's theorem (reflection principle consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If T is an axiomatizable theory extending Q with Prov_T satisfying P1–P3, and T derives Prov_T(⌜α⌝) → α, then T derives α (Theorem 197A). Equivalently, T ⊢ (Prov_T(⌜α⌝) → α) implies T ⊢ α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristic uses a fixed point for the formula Prov_T(y) → α (a self-referential 'if-then' sentence). Löb's theorem yields short proofs of second incompleteness variants and shows that only provable statements satisfy the reflection schema inside T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undefinability of truth (definability in the standard model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R(n1,...,nk) of natural numbers is definable in the standard model B if there is a formula α(x1,...,xk) such that for all n1,...,nk, R(n1,...,nk) iff |=_B α(n1,...,nk) (Definition 198A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets up the formal notion needed for Tarski-style undefinability-of-truth results: the set of true arithmetic sentences is not definable in the language of arithmetic. The text begins the formal framework for that theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language/symbol-dependent decidability facts (Presburger vs arithmetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decidability of the set of true sentences depends on language: the set of true sentences in 0,′,+,×,< (or 0,′,×) is undecidable; Presburger arithmetic (language 0,′,+) is decidable though computationally infeasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates precise boundaries: adding × yields undecidability, while addition alone (Presburger) is decidable. Use these examples when reasoning about expressiveness vs decidability.
